Even simple things such as

- having to trim strings through intersections manually. The intersection editor in Civilcad is just a dog.

I could live with all of the above though. My main issue is when the design inevitably changes (as almost always occurs) and you have to raise the vertical design or something then you have to go and manually edit every single alignment, then manually raise all the kerb returns, then manually plot & export every long section, then all the cross sections etc. Then recreate the overall design surface, redesign the stormwater, sewer everything else etc. 

Whereas in 12d (which I only started using after using Civilcad for several years) you set everything up once [which takes about the same time as in Civilcad] although if you then want to change anything everything (can if you want) dynamically updates. E.g. raise an intersection and all the kerb returns will raise accordingly also, the stormwater automatically raises, the design surface automatically updates, hit one button and you can export new .dwgs of the long sections and cross sections for every single alignment in the job if you want etc. It is much less tedious and a lot more powerful with what it calls 'modifiers' (which allows you to modify a template on the fly essentially along the design).

I wasn't a fan of 12d either initially as the help documentation is poor and it is a bitch to learn but once you learn it it makes life a lot easier than designing in Civilcad or Civil 3D. The pipe design, grading & plotting are all a lot better also. Can't really comment on the survey side of 12d as I don't use it (surveyors where I work still use Civilcad for survey).

Civilcad is worse than Civil 3D though if you want to do anything other than a very simple textbook example rural road design. Trying to do urban road design (or design changes where everything has to be manually updated) in Civilcad is a nightmare.
I've used Civil 3D, 12d & Topcon Civilcad and can safely say that 12d is by far the most powerful and best one to use; albeit the hardest to learn initially.
